newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh says Burmese refugees must go back.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh says Burmese refugees must go back.

text.p: Bangladesh, criticised over its repatriation policy for Burmese immigrants, on Monday reaffirmed that all so-called Rohingya Burmese Moslem refugees must return home.
"Bangladesh will not accept them permanently. All the refugees must go back. Our position is firm and clear," Bangladesh's Acting Foreign Secretary, Aminul Islam, told Reuters.
Canh Nguyen-Tang, UNHCR coordinator for the Bangladesh/Burma repatriation, told reporters on Sunday he had won a commitment from Bangladesh to halt the forcible repatriation of refugees.
The UNHCR official has arrived in Dhaka from his base in Rangoon as relations between Bangladesh and the U.N. agency turned tense since the on-off repatriation process resumed on July 20.
The government postponed the repatriation later that day following clashes between refugees and police and a strong protest by the UNHCR to Bangladesh.
UNHCR complained that the latest repatriation had been forcible.
Islam said on Monday: "There has been no forcible repatriation and the government would ensure that the return be voluntary."
He said authorities were trying to restart the repatriation process "as soon as possible".
"We will try our best to repatriate the 7,000 clear cases by the August 15 deadline set by the Burmese authorities."
UNHCR officials said the resumption of repatriations depended on the restoration of normality in the refugee camps.
Militant refugees on Saturday handed to Bangladeshi officials a list of conditions for their return to Burma.
They said they would only go back if Rangoon issued them with formal nationality documents, restored democracy and guaranteed human rights.
Islam said the government would continue to try to persuade the Burmese authorities to take back all the refugees, numbering 21,000.
They are the remnants of 250,000 who entered Bangladesh in 1992 to escape alleged military persecution in their home province of Arakan in west Burma.
Bangladesh argues that the remaining immigrants are economic refugees and must go home.
"If somebody thinks that they are political refugees then these people could be resettled in a third country. We have told this to UNHCR people," said Islam.
